newsitem.title: GERMANY: Hijacker wants release of Pope's would-be assassin.
newsitem.headline: Hijacker wants release of Pope's would-be assassin.

text.p: A man hijacked an Air Malta plane to Germany on Monday and police said he has demanded the release of Turkish gunman Mehmet Ali Agca, serving a life sentence in Italy after trying to assassinate the Pope in 1981.
The hijacker, who requested the services of a Turkish-speaking interpreter, also told police he was carrying a bomb.
The Boeing 737 airliner was diverted on Monday after takeoff from malta on a flight to Istanbul, Turkey.

After landing at the busy Cologne-Bonn airport 15 km (10 miles) south of the German industrial city of Cologne, it stood at a freight section and German police quickly established contact with the hijacker.
"He wants to give a television interview and then give himself up," police spokesman Werner Schmidt told reporters at the airport.
Pope John Paul was shot in the hand and abdomen as he rode in an open jeep before thousands at his general audience in St Peter's Square in Rome in 1981. Emergency surgery saved his life.
Agca, whom the Pope later forgave publicly and visited in jail, was wrestled to the ground by pilgrims, including a nun, and is serving a life sentence in Italy.
"The assailant says he has got a bomb with him. We are still negoatiating with him," Schmidt said.
He had also requested that a human rights group come to the plane to help to mediate, police said.
German police said there were 74 passengers and five crew on the airliner, when it landed. Five left the plane, among them a woman with heart problems.
"Police have started a dialogue with the hijacker and I hope that will prove constructive," Heinz Gombel, chief executive of the airport, told reporters.
Maltese state-owned airline Air Malta said soon after the plane landed that the situation on board was "reported to be calm".

Air Malta spokesman John Saliba said the plane left Malta for Istanbul at 23.45 GMT and was diverted to Cologne "following a situation that developed on board and demands made by one of the passengers."
Most of the passengers on the plane were not Maltese.
The hijacking was the first involving an Air Malta aircraft since the airline was formed in the early 1970s and the first hijack of a flight originating in Malta.
Air Malta has a growing network of services to Europe, North Africa and the Middle East including three weekly flights to Turkey.
